card.chief_complaint: abrupt regular fast heartbeat with lightheadedness

ask.changes_what: Positive: prioritise symptom-rhythm correlation (event/loop recorder) and teach vagal manoeuvres. Negative: does not exclude arrhythmia; monitor if symptoms are recurrent or concerning.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use a 'gradual' description to dismiss palpitations accompanied by syncope, chest pain, or known structural heart disease.
ask.escalation_warning: Abrupt palpitations with syncope, exertional onset, or a family history of sudden death need ECG and cardiology assessment for VT/pre-excitation, not reassurance.
ask.how: Ask whether episodes start 'like a switch' within one beat and stop just as suddenly, versus building up and fading over minutes. Ask what the patient was doing at onset, whether vagal manoeuvres (breath-hold, straining, cold water) stop it, and how long episodes last.
ask.negative_finding: Gradual onset and offset suggests sinus tachycardia (anxiety, exertion, secondary causes); the 2009 RCE found no historical feature other than neck pounding that reliably excludes a significant arrhythmia.
ask.pitfalls: Patients often cannot judge onset speed; AF may also start abruptly. The RCE found episodes lasting under 5 minutes made arrhythmia slightly less likely (LR 0.38), so duration and onset pattern should be weighed together.
ask.positive_finding: Sudden-onset, sudden-offset rapid regular palpitations, especially if terminated by vagal manoeuvres, are the classic description of re-entrant SVT and are widely used to prioritise rhythm monitoring.
ask.prerequisites: Patient has had at least one episode they can describe; a recorded rhythm during symptoms remains the reference.
ask.rationale: Abrupt onset and offset helps distinguish SVT from sinus tachycardia or anxiety, guiding acute management.
ask.title: Abrupt onset and abrupt termination of palpitations (vs gradual)

ask.changes_what: Positive: diagnose probable AVNRT - teach vagal manoeuvres, refer for EP study/ablation. Negative: look for other arrhythmia or non-arrhythmic causes; prolonged monitoring still needed.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use to reassure a patient with wide-complex tachycardia, syncope, or structural heart disease - the sign does not distinguish VT with cannon waves.
ask.escalation_warning: Neck pounding with haemodynamic compromise, syncope, or a wide-complex rhythm needs immediate ECG and acute arrhythmia management.

evidence.reference_standard: Electrophysiologic study defining AVNRT vs other tachycardia mechanisms
evidence.target_condition: AV nodal reentrant tachycardia - visible neck pulsations during palpitations

ask.how: Ask whether, during attacks, the patient feels a rapid regular pounding or 'shirt-collar flutter' in the neck, and whether others have seen the neck pulsating. If the patient is in tachycardia now, inspect the neck for rapid regular jugular pulsations (frog sign) caused by atrial contraction against closed AV valves.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of the neck-pounding sensation makes AVNRT unlikely (LR 0.07, 95% CI 0.03-0.19) but says nothing about other arrhythmias such as AF or VT.
ask.pitfalls: The estimate derives from a single electrophysiology-lab study with very wide confidence intervals; cannon A waves also occur in VT with AV dissociation and complete heart block.
ask.positive_finding: A regular rapid-pounding sensation in the neck strongly favours AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia (LR 177, 95% CI 25-1251); visible neck pulsations are a weaker pointer (LR 2.68).
ask.prerequisites: History of recurrent palpitations; direct observation requires an ongoing episode.
ask.rationale: Frog sign suggests AVNRT, which would prioritize vagal maneuvers and EP referral if present.
ask.title: Regular rapid pounding in the neck / visible neck pulsations during episodes (frog sign)

ask.changes_what: Positive: obtain ECG, telemetry and consider admission/monitoring for arrhythmia; negative: no change in cardiac-syncope probability.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of palpitations to de-escalate a syncope work-up in patients with structural heart disease, abnormal ECG, exertional or supine syncope.
ask.escalation_warning: Palpitations followed by syncope in a patient with known heart disease, family history of sudden death or an abnormal ECG warrants monitored observation and cardiology input.

evidence.citation: Berecki-Gisolf J, Sheldon A, Wieling W, et al. Identifying cardiac syncope based on clinical history: a literature-based model tested in four independent datasets. PLoS One. 2013;8(11):e75255.
evidence.location: Table 2 (Palpitations row), PMC3815402 open-access full text
evidence.population: Pooled derivation sample from 7 published syncope cohorts (Italy, Switzerland, Canada, USA); 468 cardiac and 1768 non-cardiac syncope patients with palpitation data
evidence.reference_standard: Final cause of syncope by each study's standardized diagnostic criteria (ESC-based work-up, EP study/tilt where used)
evidence.target_condition: Cardiac (arrhythmic or structural) syncope vs non-cardiac syncope

ask.how: Ask the patient (and any witness) whether they felt a racing, pounding or fluttering heartbeat in the seconds to minutes before losing consciousness, and whether it was rapid and regular or irregular. Distinguish it from the generic 'heart pounding' of a vasovagal prodrome that comes with warmth, nausea and sweating.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of palpitations does not exclude cardiac syncope; pooled literature LR for absence is about 1.0, so it changes little.
ask.pitfalls: In pooled derivation data palpitations were reported as often by non-cardiac (11%) as cardiac (8%) syncope patients, because vasovagal prodromes also include a pounding heart; the item behaves differently in patients with vs without heart disease (Alboni 2001).
ask.positive_finding: In the largest pooled literature sample (Berecki-Gisolf 2013; 468 cardiac vs 1768 non-cardiac syncope episodes) palpitations before syncope did not discriminate: LR+ 0.74, and the variable was excluded from the final model (p = 0.06). The EGSYS score nonetheless assigns palpitations +4 points, so a score-based workflow and this pooled estimate disagree. Treat palpitations as a prompt to characterise the episode (abrupt onset and offset, absence of autonomic prodrome, structural heart disease) rather than as independent evidence of arrhythmic syncope.
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to recall the prodrome; corroborate with a witness where possible.
ask.rationale: Palpitations before syncope increases concern for arrhythmic syncope, prompting closer monitoring.
ask.title: Palpitations immediately preceding syncope

ask.changes_what: Positive: ECG, electrolytes and rhythm capture, then trigger withdrawal with follow-up; negative: proceed to ambulatory monitoring based on symptom pattern, not to reassurance.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use a stimulant history to explain palpitations with syncope, chest pain, known structural heart disease or an abnormal ECG.
ask.escalation_warning: Cocaine/amphetamine-associated palpitations with chest pain, hypertension or wide-complex rhythm require ACS and toxicology pathways; alcohol withdrawal with tachycardia needs withdrawal management.
ask.how: Ask non-judgementally about the 24-48 h before the palpitations: caffeine/energy drinks (amount), decongestants, inhaled or oral beta-agonists, thyroid hormone, cocaine/amphetamines/MDMA, cannabis, nicotine, and alcohol quantity (binge in the preceding day or two) or abrupt cessation of alcohol/benzodiazepines; ask about weight-loss or 'pre-workout' supplements.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of exposures removes a reversible trigger but does not lower the probability of a primary arrhythmia; documented symptom-rhythm correlation is still required in recurrent palpitations.
ask.pitfalls: Attributing palpitations to caffeine or anxiety without a rhythm strip misses AF and SVT (cardiac cause in 43% of 190 consecutive palpitations patients, Weber 1996 Abstract); patients under-report alcohol and illicit drugs.
ask.positive_finding: A temporal link to a stimulant, sympathomimetic or alcohol binge supports sinus tachycardia, ectopy or 'holiday heart' AF as the mechanism, and in cocaine/amphetamine use raises ischaemia and ventricular arrhythmia risk.
ask.prerequisites: Privacy and, when relevant, a urine drug screen or ethanol level to corroborate; check the pulse or rhythm strip during symptoms if ongoing.
ask.rationale: Recent stimulant or alcohol use can trigger arrhythmias and may change management or counseling.
ask.title: Stimulant/substance exposure: caffeine, energy drinks, decongestants, beta-agonists, cocaine/amphetamines, alcohol binge (holiday heart), recent withdrawal

examine.changes_what: Irregular pulse during symptoms: obtain ECG for AF and anticoagulation decision; regular fast pulse with abrupt stop: pursue SVT with monitoring/EP referral.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not substitute pulse palpation for an ECG when the patient is symptomatic and monitoring is available; do not rely on a patient's self-count in syncope.
examine.escalation_warning: Pulse >150/min with hypotension, chest pain, dyspnea or altered mentation is an unstable tachyarrhythmia needing immediate ECG/monitoring and possible cardioversion.

evidence.citation: Cooke G, Doust J, Sanders S. Is pulse palpation helpful in detecting atrial fibrillation? A systematic review. J Fam Pract 2006;55:130-134.
evidence.population: 3 studies, 2385 patients, predominantly elderly primary care/screening populations
evidence.quote: Pooled sensitivity was 94% (95% confidence interval [CI], 84%-97%) and pooled specificity was 72% (95% CI, 69%-75%)

evidence.citation: Cooke G, Doust J, Sanders S. Is pulse palpation helpful in detecting atrial fibrillation? A systematic review. J Fam Pract 2006;55:130-134.
evidence.population: 3 studies, 2385 patients, predominantly elderly primary care/screening populations
evidence.quote: The pooled positive likelihood ratio was 3.39, while the pooled negative likelihood ratio was 0.10.

examine.how: During an episode, palpate the radial pulse (or auscultate the apex) for a full 60 seconds: note the rate, whether the rhythm is regular, regularly irregular (dropped beats) or irregularly irregular, and whether it stops abruptly or slows gradually. Teach the patient to do the same or to record with a smartwatch/single-lead device between visits.
examine.negative_finding: A regular pulse during symptoms makes AF unlikely (LR- 0.10). A normal rate and rhythm while symptomatic argues against an arrhythmic cause of that episode.
examine.pitfalls: The pooled data are for pulse irregularity versus ECG (largely elderly screening), not for rate or termination pattern, which are unquantified. Frequent ectopy and sinus arrhythmia mimic AF; fast rates make irregularity hard to feel.
examine.positive_finding: An irregularly irregular pulse has pooled sensitivity 0.94 and specificity 0.72 for AF (LR+ 3.4). A regular pulse at 150-250/min that stops abruptly suggests SVT; occasional dropped/early beats suggest ectopy.
examine.prerequisites: Symptoms present at the time of examination, or the patient trained to self-check; a 12-lead ECG or rhythm strip should be obtained simultaneously whenever possible.
examine.rationale: Palpating the pulse during symptoms confirms rate and regularity, helping to distinguish SVT from AF or VT.
examine.title: Palpate/auscultate the pulse (or have the patient count/record it) DURING an episode: rate, regularity, abrupt termination

examine.changes_what: Termination: re-entrant SVT, arrange EP/ablation discussion; transient block unmasking atrial activity: flutter/AT/AF pathway; no response in wide QRS: manage as VT.
examine.contraindications: Unstable tachycardia (synchronised cardioversion instead); carotid massage contraindicated with bruit, carotid disease, or TIA/stroke or MI within 3 months; Valsalva avoided in acute MI, severe aortic stenosis, recent eye/neurosurgery or retinal detachment.
examine.do_not_use_when: Hemodynamic instability (hypotension, ischaemic chest pain, pulmonary edema, altered consciousness) - cardiovert instead; carotid massage contraindications as above.
examine.escalation_warning: Wide-complex tachycardia, pre-excited AF, or any deterioration during the maneuver requires immediate ACLS management; post-termination pauses/bradycardia need monitoring.
examine.how: With a rhythm strip running, have the patient strain against a closed glottis (or blow into a 10 mL syringe/manometer to 40 mmHg) for 15 s semi-recumbent, then lie flat with passive leg raise for 15 s (modified Valsalva); or apply carotid sinus massage 5-10 s one side. Watch for abrupt termination, transient AV slowing unmasking flutter/P waves, gradual slowing, or no change.
examine.negative_finding: No response does not exclude SVT (Valsalva terminates only a minority); gradual slowing that resumes suggests sinus tachycardia; a wide-complex tachycardia unaffected by vagal maneuvers should be treated as VT.
examine.pitfalls: Termination requires an adequately performed strain (40 mmHg for 15 s), which patients often fail; without a running ECG the transient slowing that reveals flutter is missed. Vagal maneuvers can rarely provoke bradyarrhythmia or, with carotid massage, embolic stroke.
examine.positive_finding: Abrupt termination to sinus rhythm indicates an AV-node-dependent re-entrant SVT (AVNRT/AVRT); transient AV block with persisting atrial activity (flutter waves, P waves at unchanged rate) indicates atrial flutter, atrial tachycardia or AF.
examine.prerequisites: Continuous ECG recording during the maneuver; hemodynamically stable patient; IV access and adenosine/defibrillator available; auscultate carotids before massage.
examine.rationale: Response to vagal maneuvers can terminate SVT and is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
examine.title: Response of ongoing palpitations to Valsalva/modified Valsalva or carotid massage: abrupt termination vs transient slowing vs none

examine.changes_what: Chaotic irregular pattern: obtain ECG/monitoring for AF and assess stroke risk. Regular rapid pattern: pursue SVT/VT work-up. Skipped beats with normal ECG: likely benign ectopy.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use the tapped rhythm to withhold ECG or monitoring in patients with syncope, chest pain, dyspnoea, or known heart disease.
examine.escalation_warning: A rapid irregular pattern in a patient with stroke risk factors, or any pattern with syncope, warrants same-day ECG and rhythm documentation.
examine.how: Ask the patient to tap the rhythm of an episode on the table or their chest with a finger. Note whether it is fast and perfectly regular, fast and chaotic/irregular, or normal-rate with an occasional pause followed by a heavy beat ('skipped beat'). Compare with the rhythm you palpate or see on ECG if symptoms are present.
examine.negative_finding: An unremarkable or unreproducible tap pattern does not exclude arrhythmia; the 2009 RCE concluded the clinical examination cannot exclude significant arrhythmia in most patients.
examine.pitfalls: Patients' perception of regularity is unreliable, and rapid AF can feel regular; symptom-rhythm correlation on a monitor remains the reference standard.
examine.positive_finding: A rapid, metronome-regular tap pattern is the classic description of SVT or sinus tachycardia; a chaotic irregular pattern suggests atrial fibrillation; isolated pauses with a forceful beat suggest premature beats.
examine.prerequisites: Patient able to recall and reproduce the rhythm; works best soon after an episode.
examine.rationale: Having the patient tap out the rhythm helps clarify if the arrhythmia is regular or irregular, narrowing the differential.
examine.title: Patient taps out the palpitation rhythm: regular vs irregular; rapid regular vs 'skipped beats'
